content.summary_of_the_paper:
summary:

This paper presents a learning-based framework for early exit inference.

Concretely, given a pretrained multi-exit network, the proposed method learns a separate pathway alongside the forward pass to decide where to early exit the inference.

The exit score is computed using argmax prediction, entropy, and voting, and optimized w.r.t. a multi-objective loss.

The author empirically evaluates the proposed method on three vision datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet) and two NLP datasets (SST-2 and AgNews). The results are strong on NLP datasets and CIFAR-100, but somewhat marginal on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet,
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

- The proposed learning-based model-agnostic approach to the multi-exit problem is novel and relevant.
- The paper is full of details. On the upside, this is good for reference and reproducibility.
- The authors provide sufficient empirical evaluations for the proposed method. And the experimental settings are extensively discussed.

Weakness:

- Results on Image classification. While the proposed method demonstrated strong performance on NLP tasks. For example in Table 1, there are marginal differences between EENet and MSDNet on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.
- Clarity:
    - In my opinion, the clarity of this paper can be further improved for a smoother reading experience. In the method section, especially section 3.2, mathematical equations are sometimes directly provided without many intuitive explanations. Without narratives it could be a bit hard to digest these formulas and why they are designed this way.
    - On the downside, the extensive details provided in the paper could distract away the main gist of the story.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and Quality:
- My main concern is with the method section; please see the weakness section for more details.

Novelty:
- The proposed method is interesting and seems novel.

Reproducibility:
- The paper contains extensive details about the design and experimental setting, and the bottom line on page 6 also indicates that the authors will open source the code.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I find the proposed method novel and interesting, though a bit complex in nature. My main concern is that the clarity of the method section could be further improved and that the performance gain on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet seems marginal. I will provide a conservative rating at the moment but will likely raise it based on the author's rebuttal.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Official Response to the Comments of Reviewer 76WR
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for their constructive comments.

For comment (1),

EENet provides consistently better performance in image/text classification tasks on five different benchmark datasets. As pointed out by the reviewer, the performance gains on CIFAR10 and ImageNet are less significant compared to the improvements in other datasets, especially SST-2 and AgNews. We observe gains thanks to both score and distribution optimization on these datasets whereas the effect was not as strong for CIFAR10 and ImageNet experiments.

For comment (2),

We thank the reviewer for pointing out the issues related to the presentation. (For a smoother reading experience, we will revise the notation and clarify the ambiguities in the methodology section by providing further explanations for the equations in our next version.)

To enable the method, authors take a  neural network and inject multiple classification branches distributed equally through the depth. During inference, the network exists if its utility scoring function exceeds the threshold. The method is compared against 3 other works.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The problem is important and the field is active.
- The method outperforms 3 other techniques selected in the paper.

Weaknesses/questions:

- Paper doesn't compare with more recent works in the field of adaptive inference: [1]-[5]. Even more works are summarized in the survey [6]. 
- In the abstract authors mention that most methods employ hand-tuned or manual rule-based early exit policies. However, I don't see how the proposed method is not hand-tuned and not manual. 
- In the end of section 2, authors mention that EENet is the first to learn optimal early exit policies. Optimality is a tricky point. Could authors prove optimization for their algorithm? 
-  Section 3.2 is confusing. For example, not clear what does $g$ stands for and if it is different from $q$. Not clear when the exit is performed, Figure 2 has all stages enabled.
- Is the method flexible enough is not clear. For example, a new budget constrain will require retraining (eq 14), is it correct?
- Experiments:
    - Method is compared to only 3 other techniques. Were these techniques reimplemented or values are from the original papers?  
    - Comparison to more recent works on adaptive computation is necessary, please see provided references (at lest cnn/transformers for vision). 


[1] Michael Figurnov, Maxwell D Collins, Yukun Zhu, Li Zhang, Jonathan Huang, Dmitry Vetrov, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Spatially adaptive computation time for residual networks. In CVPR, 2017.

display_title: Official Response to the Comments of Reviewer BYsj

content.title: Official Response to the Comments of Reviewer BYsj
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for their constructive comments and for sharing related references. We would like to emphasize that EENet optimizes the early exit policy for a trained large multi-exit DNN model and it is augmented to the DNN model to control the scheduling of early exiting under the given average inference budget per sample.

For comment (1),

We thank the reviewer for sharing a list of relevant studies. As pointed out by the reviewer, these studies perform adaptive inference using various techniques such as sparsification, pruning and adaptive inference graphs. However, all of these methods require training the backbone model each time whenever the budget constraints change whereas, in our approach, the backbone is always the same independent of the inference budget. If the resource constraints change, only the EENet model is re-trained, which has computationally negligible training cost since the network has a very small number of parameters as shown in Table 4. Therefore, in our comparisons, we did not provide the results for papers that target improving the training of backbone multi-exit models or designing efficient DNN model architectures.

For comment (2),

We thank the reviewer for this comment. Our method introduces hyperparameters to define the architecture of EENet, which are selected based on the validation performance and hence can’t be considered as a manual or hand-tuned design choice. On the other hand, e.g., defining confidence based on the agreement among exit classifiers as in PABEE [1], or using maximum prediction score and assuming geometric exit distribution as in MSDNet [2] are manual decisions, and does not involve any optimization.

For comment (3),

We thank the reviewer for this comment. We define optimality in the context of maximizing the validation performance while satisfying inference budget constraints. We validate the effectiveness of EENet with experimental results. The amount of theoretical analysis in early exiting for adaptive inference is very limited and we leave this for a future study. (We will revise the terminology to avoid ambiguities in our next version).

For comment (4),

We thank the reviewer for this comment and would like to clarify this issue. The functions denoted as $g_k$ (k: exit index) are exit utility scoring functions as explained in Eq. 8 and 9. This function takes the confidence score vector ($\boldsymbol{a}_k$), prediction score vector ($\boldsymbol{\hat{y}}_k$) and the exit utility scores obtained at previous exits ($\boldsymbol{b}_k$), and returns the exit utility score. $\boldsymbol{q}_k$ is the target variable for this function and it represents the correctness of a prediction as explained in Eq. 3. In other words, it is one if the prediction is correct and zero otherwise. In Figure 2, all exits are enabled since during the training of EENet, all exits are in operation, and the actual early exiting is only performed during inference.

For comment (5),

We thank the reviewer for this comment. In our approach, only EENet model requires re-training and the large multi-exit DNN model can be used again. Therefore, our method is significantly more flexible compared to other studies that require training the full system for a new budget constraint. 

For comment (6),

We thank the reviewer for this comment. We performed experiments using the released codes by the authors of the corresponding techniques. As mentioned in the response for comment #1, we didn’t compare EENet with studies that involve optimizing the training of multi-exit models or designing new DNN model architectures instead of optimizing an early exit policy.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a novel early-exit policy optimization framework that learns an optimal early-exit policy for adaptive inference. They first claim that it is better to learn: (I) what number of exits K is most suitable, (II) where to exit, and (III) how to optimize. More concretely, EENet defines a more accurate exit utility score by combining three quality measures (entropy, maximum prediction confidence, and voting), demonstrating strong results in low latency scenarios.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength

(1) The definition of exit utility score sounds reasonable.

(2) EENet achieves significantly better results than previous models with BERT models. 

(3) The ablation study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed components.

## Weakness

(1) While the authors list three key questions at the beginning of Section 3, they seem to have no specific solutions for the first question e.g., what number of K is most suitable? Does EENet learn how many k to use? With a claim that previous works manually set K which is not optimal, it is better to provide a solution that can automatically learn it.

(2)  The visualization does not completely explain the winning of EENet. While the predictions for low-success classes have higher exit utility scores in Figure 3, there seem to be some other blue images on the right side of the x-axis (oranges, mountain) whose utility scores actually decreases. Can the authors elaborate more on this?

(3) There are typos here and there. For instance, in fig2, the $\alpha_1$ does not connect to anything, then why do we calculate this?

(4) What does EENet stands for? I suppose that it refers to Early Exit Net since I didn't find an explanation in the paper. However, I believe EENet is a general name that can cover all Early Exit models, which doesn't reflect any specific properties of the proposed method in the paper. It is better to change the name so that can properly reflect the characteristics of the method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed method is somewhat novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a novel early-exit policy optimization framework that learns an optimal early-exit policy for adaptive inference. Albeit the proposed method is relatively complex to use and the visualization does not completely support the design, the performance in low latency scenarios is promising. I think it can be accepted if the above weakness can be addressed further.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Official Response to the Comments of Reviewer va2R
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for their time, constructive comments and for pointing out the issues related to the presentation.

For comment (1), 

This paper presents an early exit policy optimization framework for budgeted adaptive inference. Our method optimizes the early exit scheduling for a given multi-exit DNN model and average inference budget per sample. In this work, we do not target optimizing the number or locations of early exits. 

In existing studies and also in our paper, the number and locations of early exits are set heuristically. We follow the procedure described in Section 3.1., first paragraph:

…we first inject early exit classifiers into the model at certain intermediate layers. We set the exit locations $l_k$ following the even spacing principle such that $l_k=l_0+kL$ for $k \in \{1, 2, ...K-1\}$, where $l_0$ is the location of the first exit, $L=\nfloor{\frac{N-l_0}{K-1}}$ and $l_K=N$ is the location of the last exit, i.e. the full model.

The problem of finding the optimal number and locations of exits is interesting in the sense that in general, having early exits at each layer can provide flexibility but it can be computationally expensive. We would like to note that EENet does not require having a large number of exits to perform effectively as opposed to certain recent studies such as EPNet [1] that require early exits at each layer.

For comment (2), 

We would like to provide a detailed interpretation of the results shown in Figure 3.

A trained DNN model can output prediction scores with different statistics depending on the class. For instance, this particular model outputs maximum prediction scores within the range of [0.071, 0.675] for the lizard class (low success) and [0.298, 0.999] for the orange class (high success). In this figure, we aim to visualize that EENet utility scores are better representations of prediction confidence compared to the maximum prediction scores. For instance, an exit utility score of 0.6 represents the same level of confidence for all samples in a consistent manner whereas a maximum prediction score of 0.6 would represent different levels of confidence depending on the class. To this end, we highlighted two cases:
True predictions for low-success classes have higher utility scores
False predictions for high-success classes have lower utility scores

Therefore, the statistics of EENet exit utility scores do not vary depending on the class and can be used as a consistent measure in the decision-making phase. In Figure 3, we visualized randomly selected 50 images from 10 classes. Among these, there are in total, only 4-5 images from high-success classes that have slightly lower scores even though they were correctly predicted. The reason is the fact that these predictions already have low maximum prediction scores compared to other images in their respective classes, which causes EENet to suppress the utility scores for these predictions. (We will also put these detailed interpretations in our next version.)

For comment (3),

We thank the reviewer for pointing out this issue. In Figure 2, in the first exit, \bolsymbol{a}_1 should have been connected to \mathbf{W}_1^{(sh)} as in the other exits as explained in Eq. 8. This confidence score vector contains three different measures: maximum prediction score, entropy-based score and voting-based score as explained in Eq. 5-7. (We will revise this figure, clarify the ambiguities in a few notations and other typos in the next version.)

For comment (4),

We thank the reviewer for this comment. EENet stands for EarlyExitNetwork, since the network optimizes the early exit scheduling of a trained multi-exit model given the inference budget. (We will consider revising the name of our approach in the next version.)

References:
[1] Xin Dai, Xiangnan Kong, and Tian Guo. Epnet: Learning to exit with flexible multi-branch network.
In Proceedings of the 29th ACM International Conference on Information amp; Knowledge
Management, 2020.
